title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can support foreign language teachers in creating lesson plans, and more specifically whether increasing prompt specificity improves the quality and consistency of AI-generated plans. The authors frame the problem as a practical one for language education: teachers often must design their own materials, while generative AI may help streamline that work but may also reproduce outdated or weak pedagogical practices.

The study used ChatGPT 4.0 with five zero-shot prompts of increasing specificity. The prompts were designed around a 45-minute high school Level I Spanish lesson for novice learners, with objectives tied to Costa Rican restaurant vocabulary and communicative tasks. The authors generated 10 lesson plans per prompt, producing 50 outputs total, and scored each output against 25 rubric criteria adapted from best-practice lesson design and edTPA-related expectations used in a teacher preparation context at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. They then analyzed scores, word counts, and output dissimilarity using ANOVA, Jaccard distances, NMDS, PERMANOVA, ANOSIM, and hierarchical clustering.

The main finding was that greater prompt specificity did not produce a simple linear improvement in lesson quality. Adding a lesson plan template sometimes reduced scores, while adding an explicit checklist of required criteria produced the highest average scores. The outputs were highly variable even when the same prompt was repeated, showing that ChatGPT was not deterministic and could produce both strong and weak lesson plans from identical inputs. The authors also found that some generated plans reflected outdated or anachronistic language-teaching approaches, including behaviorist or audio-lingual elements and weak treatment of cultural connections. They conclude that ChatGPT can be useful for lesson planning, but only if teachers critically evaluate outputs and are trained to refine prompts and revise AI-generated materials.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational/comparative prompt-engineering study with systematic scoring, but it is not a randomized educational impact evaluation and has no human learner outcomes. It provides useful evidence about model behavior and output quality, but credibility is limited to a descriptive lab-style design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical value for teacher planning efficiency and flags institutional risks in lesson design, but it does not demonstrate measured student learning gains or large-scale implementation effects. Its impact is therefore plausible but indirect and modest/unclear at the population level.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT 4.0 via zero-shot prompting to generate foreign language teacher lesson plans, then evaluating how prompt specificity and templates affect output quality and variability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT can substantially streamline foreign language lesson-plan creation, with generally high-quality outputs and an overall mean score up to 21.6/25 when a checklist of criteria was provided (P.5). However, increased prompt specificity did not improve quality linearly, and repeated runs of the same prompt varied widely, ranging from 16/25 to 25/25 across 10 iterations for a given prompt.
finding.measure: Rubric-based lesson plan quality scores, word count, and presence/absence of 25 lesson-plan criteria across 50 generated plans
finding.study_size: n=50 generated lesson plans (5 prompts x 10 iterations)

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights that ChatGPT outputs can reproduce anachronistic or research-rejected pedagogical practices, including weak cultural integration and occasional audio-lingual style activities, which raises concerns for teacher preparation and curriculum quality. The authors argue that teacher AI literacy and critical review are necessary because generative AI may subtly bias instructional materials toward outdated practices.
finding.measure: Presence/absence of rubric components aligned to ACTFL standards and edTPA-style lesson plan criteria; qualitative inspection of generated lesson plan features
